turn_text: The fact that the principal four met last week the house still out of session for the rest of the month are their plans for additional meetings and is there a chance you can still come to a conclusion that might make the lame duck session.

Oh, I absolutely think there's a possibility for us to come together. Our staffs are meeting almost every day and we're either meeting in person or talking on the phone. So we are working hard to be able to make that happen. And I think it's going to just take folks put in the politics at the door and talking about what needs to be done to create a bill that meets the needs of farmers, ranchers and small towns and families all across the country. We have a big diverse country and the bill needs to reflect how we address issues that every part of the country is concerned about.

Some people want to sit on the sidelines and they want to blame a person or they want to blame a issue for keeping this to come together. Is this bigger than a one-issue impasse or a one-person of the four impasse?

Absolutely, and it's unfortunate folks want to... Blaming in politics and the tax never get anything done. So I don't participate in that and Senator Roberts doesn't participate in that. So that's how we got a farm bill done with 86 votes. And it's not just about SNAP, although it's important. I'm not interested. We are saving money because of the work we did in the current Farm Bill and the economy getting better. We're saving close to $80 billion because the current work programs work and the job training programs work and the economy is getting better and so on. And so we want to keep the policies that are working going. But we have big differences in the commodity title. Yeah, I appreciate the chairman of the house being from West Texas and wanting to do everything he can for cotton, but he moves dollars, tens of millions of dollars, hundreds of millions really away from the Midwest and other growers that have seen their prices drop 50% and their costs going up and everything with trade. So that just doesn't work. And there's a big difference in the conservation title where the house cuts about a billion dollars and For those of us that are involved in major conservation efforts with water around the Great Lakes as well as land conservation, that does not have support in the Senate. And the House basically eliminated the funding for any energy title, which is also a big issue for the Midwest. So I see basically a lot of regional differences if you're in the South. mainly focused on cotton or livestock, you have a different view than if you're in the Midwest where we've got all kinds of commodities and dairy and corn and wheat and dry beans and soybeans and all the other things we grow, specialty crops, so there's just some big differences.

Well, I think it is very important to stress as Chairman Roberts said that we have work requirements right now. The law is that for people that are viewed as able-bodied adults, if they don't work or go to job training programs 20 hours a week, that they don't receive any assistance. Basically, if you're not working 20 hours a week, then the most assistance you could receive is up to three months of food assistance within a two-year period. And so the average food assistance is about $4 a day. So people are expected to work except for senior citizens, people with disabilities, children, and parents taking care of children. And so what the house does is expand more older people that would have to work. and parents with children. And so that's just not a direction that makes sense from our standpoint. And what we want to do is continue to work with states on job training and other ways which we can get people who are not already in the workforce, into the workforce, and continue what is now actually very robust work requirements that we have.
